subject: The full post-login journey as four surfaces — your homes (the list) · the estate · account settings · place settings — plus the return controls between them, the `+` that founds a place, and the account-vs-estate colour collision. Designing interfaces from Paul's rulings (BACKLOG 19 / 19b / 19c / 20); no product code written.
review_level: flow / IA (four surfaces and the graph between them), with screen-component rulings inside it

user_context.primary_user: A person who owns ONE place, has finished setup, and is returning. Two real instances: Bob (VOCABULARY.md:147, paul-stated 2026-09-05 — arriving this week, will eventually want two houses, one to each daughter) and Mom (Fernwood plus a condo she does not have yet). Neither is a switcher today; both are one-place readers who have been TOLD a second is coming. Mom is gate 3 of the release cascade and is NOT the first reader of these surfaces.
core_jobs_to_be_done: Get into my place — the reason I opened the app at all. Nothing may stand between me and it.
Know this is mine, and on a shared phone, know whose it is
Fix the small things I got wrong — the name, the colour, how you reach me — without asking a person (P: 'everything is changeable' must be TRUE)
Later, and not today: add my second place, and know today whether that is even possible
user_context.context_of_use: iPhone 414 × 848 at A+ (measured standard, 8 of 8 reports). One hand. Often at the property, where there is NO cell reception and Wi-Fi only near the house — so every one of these four surfaces will at some point be opened offline. Depth-1 attention is the measured pattern on the one instrumented reader: card faces, never opening individuals. Anything behind a disclosure is content she has not seen.

findings.observation: THE `+`, AND THE HONEST INTERACTION BEHIND IT. It cannot found a place: `scopeFor()` has zero callers, `scopeOf(env)` has 51, and the estate comes from the deployment binding. Three shapes are available and two of them are lies. (A) Don't ship it — honest, but it removes the only reason the list exists for a one-place reader and hides the roadmap from the two people who actually asked. (B) A full 'found a place' flow that ends in a message to Paul — it looks like founding, walks like founding, and is a note box in a costume. That is exactly the defect 19c is retiring on the arrival page ('That's not right ›' opening a note), reproduced on a bigger surface. Reject it. (C) One screen that says plainly what it cannot do, takes the one genuinely useful thing, and promises nothing.
findings.user_impact: This project has broken *capture must not lie* twice, once today. A control that reports a success it did not achieve costs more than a missing control, because the reader stops watching for the real one — estate/index.html's own comment block says so over the code that did it. And this is the FIRST thing Bob will reach for: he has told Paul he wants two houses.
findings.principle_invoked: Capture must not lie (CLAUDE.md) + A CTA's label must promise what the destination actually delivers, AND its corollary — when the destination is fixed, the label needs no rewrite (cross-project) + Nielsen #1 (visibility of true system status)
findings.recommendation: SHIP (C). Placement: the LAST row of the list, wearing the same row shape as a place but outlined rather than railed — so it is visibly in the family and visibly not a place. Never a floating action button (platform chrome, register-leak, and it would float over the list) and never in the header (a bare `+` in a header is glyph-only routing, which the no-glasses rule forbids). Label: `＋ Add a home` — word-led. Weight: outlined neutral (`gg-suggest-btn-neutral`), NEVER filled+✓ — the affirmative means *recorded*, and nothing is recorded by tapping this. ON TAP, one card, not a flow: (1) the truthful state in the heading slot, FIRST, above everything — in the shape of 'I can't set up a second home for you yet'; first person, named actor, no status-page noun (the 'Early days' not 'Buildout in progress' ruling already governs this register); (2) one sentence saying Paul sets each home up by hand today and is building the part that lets a person do it themselves; (3) ⛔ NO TIME PROMISE OF ANY KIND — no 'soon', no bar, no step count; s3's own source comment records that 'a few days' has already been wrong here; (4) ONE optional free-text line — 'What's the other place?' — captured verbatim, deterministic, AI-free, POSTed to `/api/feedback` with `context.type: "add-home-request"`; (5) the send button is the app's EXISTING filled Send component (`✓Send`), labelled 'Send this to Paul' — same component, not a lookalike, and the ✓ is honest because the NOTE genuinely lands; (6) success/failure reuse estate/index.html's `done(ok)` shape verbatim — the note is not cleared until the server has it, and a failure says so and leaves her words in the box. ⛔ THE FIVE THINGS THAT WOULD MAKE IT A LIE, and this list is the falsifier: ① any second entry appearing in the list after the tap — a greyed row, a 'pending' row, a 'being set up' row. A place that does not exist rendered as a place that does is the worst outcome available. ② Any future tense with a schedule attached. ③ A form that collects a NAME and an ADDRESS for the second place — collecting the shape of a place asserts the place is being made; it collects one message, not a record. ④ The filled+✓ confirmation appearing on anything but a real 2xx. ⑤ A DISABLED-looking `+`. A disabled control communicates nothing and invites tapping; it is not an honest third option. ⚠️ ON THE LABEL, which is the one judgement call here: a strict read of the CTA rule forbids 'Add a home' because the destination does not add a home. I am ruling the other way on the rule's own corollary — the label is right for the destination it WILL have, the destination is what is behind it, and the destination's first line tells the truth before anything else is read. If Paul prefers the label carry the limitation, the alternative is 'Ask about a second home', and it will have to be renamed the day founding lands.

findings.observation: THE STOP IS CONDITIONAL; THE CONTROL IS NOT — and this is the whole navigation model. Paul ruled 'login → a list of your places → tap one → estate'. Taken literally at ONE place that is a full screen listing one thing, crossed on every visit, before the app — which is R1-SC, the option the 09-02 work rejected in its own words as 'a whole screen spent on a BINARY she changes about twice a year', and it violates R1-B's criterion ('never puts anything between her and the weather card, which is both of her card opens since lap 4'). Meanwhile the OPPOSITE error is just as available: R1-SA's rule was 'absent at one grant', and applying that here makes the list vanish for exactly the readers who have one place — 100% of readers today, and both of the two people who have asked for a second. The list holds the only `+` in the product. A surface that disappears precisely when it holds the only affordance anyone needs from it is not restraint, it is a dead end.
findings.user_impact: Get this wrong in the first direction and every reader pays a screen, every visit, forever, to be told something she already knows. Get it wrong in the second and founding a second place is unreachable for everyone who might want one.
findings.principle_invoked: Friction kills — it just works (cross-project) + Meet the user at the action (cross-project) + R1-B's own criterion, which survives this scope change intact + Nielsen #8 (aesthetic and minimalist design)
findings.recommendation: MY RULING, and Paul can overrule it: sign-in resolves the person's homes and BRANCHES on how many there are. At exactly one, it lands in that place — the list is not interposed. At two or more, it lands on the list. The list is ALWAYS reachable, at any count, from the estate's return control (F5). One derived branch on `estates.length`, no flag, no stored preference, no setting. ⭐ WHAT THIS PRESERVES OF PAUL'S RULING: the entire graph is unchanged — list → tap → estate → quiet control back to the list → `+` founds the next one. What changes is only whether the list is a STOP on the way in, and at one home the answer is no because it has nothing to say. ⭐ AND THIS IS PRECISELY HOW R1-SA IS SUPERSEDED RATHER THAN WRONG. Its MECHANISM — presence derived from grant count, never a disabled state — survives and is what I have applied. Its FORM (the masthead chevron) dies, and its RULE inverts: 'absent at one' was correct for a switcher, which has nothing to do at one; this control is also the door to founding and to account settings, so it always has a job. The stop is what goes absent, not the control. FALSIFIER: with one home, sign-in reaches the place with zero intermediate taps AND the list is reachable in one tap from it. With two, sign-in reaches the list. Nothing on either surface is disabled in either state.

findings.observation: THE COLOUR COLLISION — and the answer is not a precedence rule, it is that one of the two concepts should not exist. Facts: the account's `accent` is LIVE (chosen from the 7-swatch palette at signup, stored `fw-accent`, carried on the account row, and it is what paints estate/index.html's masthead today); the estate's `identity.theme.main` is DECLARED and RULED (`paul-stated 2026-09-04` — the condo dark blue, Fernwood its green) and read by NOTHING. Two concepts, neither aware of the other, and Paul's request puts a settings control on both surfaces. ⭐ THE READER'S MODEL IS ALREADY SETTLED AND THE PRODUCT SETTLED IT: onboarding says, in shipped copy every walker has read, *'Pick a colour — it's the one YOUR PLACE will open in.'* Colour is a property of the place. The account-level `accent` is not a design decision anyone made — it exists because at signup there was exactly one place, so account-colour and place-colour were indistinguishable.
findings.user_impact: An account-level colour is not merely redundant at two places — it is actively harmful. At two homes the masthead colour is the fastest pre-literate 'which one am I in' signal available, and it is the only one that survives at half-engagement without reading. One colour across both homes destroys that signal and makes two different places look identical. That is a wayfinding loss paid to preserve a value nobody chose.
findings.principle_invoked: One engine, one verdict (fernwood canon — two stores for one displayed value) + Norman: a signifier must distinguish the thing it is attached to + Ornament earns its place (cross-project) + Nielsen #4 (consistency and standards)
findings.recommendation: RULE: COLOUR IS PER-PLACE. One concept, one store, one picker. Consequences, all of them cheap: ① The colour picker lives in PLACE settings, second item, exactly as Paul ruled. ② ACCOUNT settings carries NO colour picker. That is the answer to 19c's warning 'do not build two colour pickers before answering it' — build one, and it is on the place. ③ The signup swatch does not move and its copy does not change, because it already says the right thing — which is the strongest available evidence the ruling is correct. ④ The existing account `accent` becomes the founding home's colour in a one-time, deterministic migration with no reader-visible event. ⑤ `identity.theme.main` becomes the read path and the account `accent` its seed at founding; the engineering shape is not mine, the rule is *one value renders and it is per-place*. ⑥ THE LIST BELONGS TO NO PLACE, so it wears none of them — the product's existing green-on-cream. That is honest and it makes the coloured rows on it read as the places' own. ⚠️ IF PAUL WANTS A PERSONAL COLOUR ANYWAY, the second-best rule, stated so it is not invented ad hoc later: the place's colour wins wherever a place is on screen, and the account colour appears ONLY on the two surfaces that belong to no place (the list and account settings). Coherent, but it buys nothing and costs a second concept. FALSIFIER: change a colour at a home and that home renders it; no other home changes; and there is exactly one control in the product that writes a colour.

findings.observation: 'ONE SETTINGS SURFACE REACHABLE FROM TWO PARENTS MUST KNOW ITS ORIGIN' — the requirement is real, and the cheapest correct answer is to not create it. Account settings and place settings hold different objects: one is per-person and there is exactly one of it; the other is per-place and there will be N. Building them as one screen with a mode flag is how the colour collision in F3 becomes permanent, and it manufactures a stored origin that can be wrong.
findings.user_impact: Paul asked how it reads to a person, not just how it is stored. A screen that wears two hats is a screen where the reader cannot predict what 'back' does — and at depth-1, a back control whose destination she has to infer is a control she will not use, which makes the settings pages one-way trips.
findings.principle_invoked: Scope is communicated by where you tap, not auto-detected (cross-project) + Nielsen #6 (recognition over recall) + Norman: mapping — a control's destination should be visible, not remembered
findings.recommendation: TWO SURFACES, ONE PARENT EACH. Account settings is reached ONLY from the list; back → the list. Place settings is reached ONLY from inside a place; back → that place. The origin requirement then dissolves — there is no ambiguity to store and no path on which the back control can be wrong. ⭐ HOW IT READS TO A PERSON: the back control NAMES ITS DESTINATION IN WORDS, and the destination is different in each case, so she never has to remember how she got there — she reads it. From a home: `‹ Fernwood` (the place's own name — most specific wins, the same rule the top bar already runs on, VOCABULARY §3b). From the list: `‹ Your homes`. The page's own heading confirms it: place settings is titled with the place's name, account settings with 'Your account'. ⛔ AND THE CONSTRAINT THAT KEEPS IT TRUE: the list row does exactly ONE thing — enter the place. No long-press, no inline edit affordance, no per-row gear. Everything about a place is edited inside it. The moment a second route into place settings exists, the ambiguity Paul flagged comes back and it comes back as stored state. FALSIFIER: there is no code path that renders one settings surface with two different back targets. If one appears, the surfaces were wrongly merged.

findings.observation: THE QUIET CONTROL NEAR THE TOP — form, wording, placement, and its exact cost. Constraints stack up hard: quiet and unintrusive (Paul), must not compete with the jump strip (5 of 5 taps, the one affordance she takes every time), must not leak ops-dashboard register, must be readable without glasses, must be a 44px target, must not route by glyph alone, and the masthead already has a ruled job — it answers 'where am I', most specific wins.
findings.user_impact: This control is how a person discovers that more than one home is even possible. If it is a chevron on a title, she has to guess the title is tappable — a discoverability tax on a reader whose measured behaviour is depth-1 and who has never explored anything in this app. If it is loud, it competes with the thing she came for.
findings.principle_invoked: Prefer the platform's native control over an app reimplementation (cross-project) + Glyphs follow the journal voice, not the dashboard voice (fernwood) + For a low-exploration user an affordance must live where she already looks (fernwood candidate) + a CTA's label must promise its destination (cross-project)
findings.recommendation: ONE UTILITY ROW INSIDE THE MASTHEAD BAND, ABOVE THE h1. Left: `‹ Your homes`. Right: `Settings`. Both word-led, both ~0.82rem, white at ~0.8 opacity on the accent, both 44px tall by `::after` (the app's existing `.tap44` mechanism — reuse it, invent nothing). Then the h1 beneath, unchanged and still the largest thing on the screen. TOTAL COST: about 22px at A+, stated honestly because that is the entire price and it is the only thing being spent. WHY ABOVE THE h1 AND NOT BELOW: 'where am I' must stay first and largest; a line above it reads as the breadcrumb it is, and it is where the eye and the thumb already go on every iOS screen — which is the native-control rule doing real work rather than being cited. WHY NOT THE MASTHEAD ITSELF (R1-SA): it double-books the one element VOCABULARY §3b gives a single job, it cannot carry `+`, and it routes on a chevron. WHY NOT A HAMBURGER OR A GEAR GLYPH: register-leak (that is SaaS admin chrome on a field-journal surface) plus glyph-only routing. ⚠️ ON THE WORD 'SETTINGS': it is a platform word every phone owner knows and it names a drawer of preferences, not a management function over a life — so it clears §4's test that killed 'estate manager', 'hub', 'portal' and 'dashboard'. I recommend keeping it and flagging it to content-steward rather than inventing a warmer synonym; 'About this place' would promise content and deliver controls. ⛔ The same two-control row appears on the LIST (`Your account ›` at the BOTTOM of the list, not the top — anything above the places competes with the only thing she came for, and at one home a top-anchored settings control would outrank the single place).

findings.observation: THE LIST AT ONE HOME — what is on it, and whether a list of one is the right rendering. Paul asked directly. Related: the surface's own title is DOUBLE-BOOKED right now — VOCABULARY §3b ratifies 'your homes' as the product-level greeting (`paul-stated 2026-09-02`) while BACKLOG 19b calls it 'your places' (`2026-09-06`, correctly rejecting `property` but landing on a third noun). §3b also warns, in its own words, that 'your homes' over a single card 'reads oddly'.
findings.user_impact: A list of one that apologises for itself ('You have 1 place', an empty-state frame, a greyed second slot) teaches the reader the product is incomplete on the surface whose job is to make her feel she has arrived. A list of one that reads as a shelf teaches her the shelf can hold more — which is the belief the `+` needs.
findings.principle_invoked: Make every surface read at half-engagement (fernwood) + Ornament earns its place (cross-project) + Never surface an empty module — one honest card beats a skeleton loader (CLAUDE.md) + Nielsen #4
findings.recommendation: YES, A LIST OF ONE IS RIGHT — because it is not a screen she is made to cross (F2), and because it is the only carrier of `+`. THE ROW: the home's name in her words exactly, no title-casing (the mom seat's lowercase 'the condo' surviving every screen is recorded as the thing that told her the app was listening — do not break that here); beneath it, ONE quiet line, the town and state from `addressParts` if present, and nothing at all if absent. ⛔ NEVER the full street address on this surface — the list is not a receipt, and a street address on a shared-device shelf is a disclosure doing no work. A 4px left rail in that home's colour: it is a signifier, not ornament, because it predicts what the next screen will look like and it teaches the colour↔place mapping before there are two. ⛔ NOT ON THE ROW: any badge, count, status, 'last opened', or 'needs attention'. All ops chrome, none of it true. THE HEADING: plural, always, matched EXACTLY to the string on the return control in F5 — a label must promise its destination, so the control and the page title are one string or the journey has a seam in it. My recommendation on the noun, flagged as Paul's since it is a naming ruling and not a UX one: use §3b's ratified **'Your homes'**, plural even at one. §3b's oddness warning is real but mild, and the plural does affordance work — a plural heading over one card is itself the quietest possible statement that more than one is possible, which is exactly what the `+` beneath it needs the reader to already believe. If Paul prefers 'places', the only hard requirement is that ONE noun wins and `check-vocabulary.py` is told, because two live words for one surface is §5's defect class arriving fresh.

findings.observation: ACCOUNT SETTINGS — and its lead item is not a preference, it is the highest-stakes field in the product. `#contactpick` is answered on screen ONE of five, it is the one radio group with a PRE-SELECTED default ('Email me', checked), the 'Please don't' branch carries a real disclosed consequence (there is no password reset, so Paul-by-hand is the only route back in), and it is never shown again. TWO seats said so unprompted and independently: strict — *'I made a decision about how a stranger can reach me, and then it disappeared from view entirely. I'd have liked to see it once more'*; mom — *'what I do NOT see anywhere on this last screen is my username, my colour choice, or how I said Paul should reach me'*. It is also the field no synthetic seat can exercise, because no seat can decline.
findings.user_impact: The cost of a wrong value here is not friction, it is the account. And because it is pre-selected, the most likely wrong value is the one nobody chose. A person who wanted 'please don't' and never noticed the default has granted a permission she did not give, and has no surface anywhere in the product on which to discover it.
findings.principle_invoked: Every ASK says USE · NOT-use · WHO SEES IT · reversibility (paul-stated 2026-09-05) + 'Everything is changeable' must be TRUE (CLAUDE.md rule 5) + Nielsen #3 (user control and freedom) and #9 (recognise and recover)
findings.recommendation: ORDER, top to bottom: ① **HOW TO REACH YOU** — the `#contactpick` component itself with the current value selected, plus the email/phone rows, plus the consequence line inline exactly as onboarding carries it. This is the reason account settings ships in pass 1. ② **USERNAME** — shown, not editable. Shown because a seat asked whether it saved, and because VOCABULARY §3b makes it 'the only part of an account other people can see', so on a shared device it says whose account this is. Editing it is a key change and is out of scope; say nothing about editing rather than offering a control that half-works. ③ **PASSWORD** — conditional on the Worker having a change path, which I did not verify. If it has one, a change row. If it does not, the row still appears and states what is true — there is no reset, email Paul — because a settings page that silently omits the password answers the wrong question when she goes looking for it. ④ NO COLOUR PICKER (F3). ⑤ Sign out (F10). Back control: `‹ Your homes`. ⛔ NOTHING ELSE. No delete-account, no export, no notification preferences, no people, no sharing — none of them exist, and a settings page listing things it cannot do is a menu of disappointments.

findings.observation: PLACE SETTINGS — contents, order, and the save loop. Paul ruled it begins with the NAME and the COLOUR. 19c also correctly identifies it as the destination the arrival page's two placeholder links have been waiting for: 'That's not right ›' and 'Change the order ›' currently open a NOTE BOX, which is the F12 workaround for the fact that re-entering onboarding's `step()`/`K_STEP` walks the reader forward through the confirm and the ranking again.
findings.user_impact: This is the single best demonstration in the product that the app listens: she changes the name or the colour, taps back, and the masthead she is returning to is already different. That is a loop-close she cannot misread, and it costs nothing to build because both values already paint that header.
findings.principle_invoked: Save-success at the surface, not at the destination (cross-project) — SHARPENED, see below + Meet the user at the action (cross-project) + Close the loop on the ENTITY, not with a status tracker (fernwood candidate) + 'Everything is changeable' must be TRUE
findings.recommendation: ORDER: ① **NAME** — pre-filled with her exact current string; reuse `#pname` as a COMPONENT (maxlength 60, no forced title-casing); one short varied changeability clause beneath it. ② **COLOUR** — the same seven-swatch `#swatches` component, current selected. ③ **WHERE IT IS** — the address; reuse the s2 FIELD GROUP as a component, never the s2 SCREEN with its step machinery, lede and forward button (F12's ruling — an edit route must not re-enter the sequential flow). ④ **WHAT I'LL BUILD FIRST** — the ranking, reusing `#interests`. Then STOP: no people, no sharing, no delete, no export. ⭐ SAVE AND RETURN, and this is the sharpening the cross-project rule earns here: ONE 'Save changes' button at the bottom in the ratified filled+✓ grammar, its success shown AT that button — and then the back control returns her to the estate where the change is ALREADY VISIBLE. The strongest possible save-success is a destination that has already changed; the confirmation at the button exists only to cover the moment before she taps back. ⛔ OFFLINE (F9): the fields are not cleared and the page does not navigate until a real 2xx; a failure says so and leaves her words. Reuse estate/index.html's `done(ok)` verbatim — do not mint a second vocabulary for the same event. ⛔ ZERO DISCLOSURES on this page. All four items on the card face. A settings page is the most tempting surface in any app to build an accordion, and at depth-1 an accordion is a page she has not read.

findings.observation: ALL FOUR OF THESE SURFACES WILL BE OPENED WHERE THERE IS NO NETWORK. The property has no cell reception and Wi-Fi only near the house, and it is a permanent premise, not a caveat. The list, both settings pages and the estate all read server-held values (`/api/grant/whoami` returns name, accent, address, addressParts, ranked, contactPref). estate/index.html already solves this correctly — render from localStorage instantly, reconcile from the server, server wins on disagreement, and SILENCE on a transport failure so an offline reader keeps her cached view rather than being told her place is empty.
findings.user_impact: A settings page that shows a spinner, or that renders empty and then says 'couldn't load', is a settings page nobody at the property can use — and the reader most likely to open it there is the one standing in front of the thing she wants to correct.
findings.principle_invoked: THE SITE'S PHYSICAL PREMISE (CLAUDE.md, paul-stated 2026-08-31) + Static visuals lie on dynamic surfaces (cross-project) + Nielsen #1
findings.recommendation: Copy estate/index.html's `reconcile()` pattern onto all four surfaces rather than writing a second one. Specifically: the LIST renders from the cached `estates` array immediately and never shows a loading state for a one-item list; both settings pages pre-fill from cache and correct on reconcile; a save attempted offline reports the truth and holds her input. ⚠️ AND THE ONE NEW HAZARD: a save that fails offline must not leave the local cache updated while the server is behind — that is the surface telling her the change took when it did not, which is the same class as the cleared-textarea incident. Local cache updates on 2xx only, exactly as the note path does.

findings.observation: SIGN OUT BELONGS ON ACCOUNT SETTINGS AND IT IS A TRAP AS THINGS STAND. The shared-device case is documented in this repo, not hypothetical — Paul shared his phone with Mom until 07-28, and the owner guard in estate/index.html exists because a shared device once resumed a different person's progress and showed them an address they had never typed. But there is no password reset: a reader who signs out and cannot remember her password has exactly one route back, and it is Paul by hand — and if she chose 'please don't contact me', she has closed even that from her side.
findings.user_impact: Signing out is the one genuinely irreversible-feeling action available in the product, and today it would be offered next to a colour picker with no indication that it is different in kind.
findings.principle_invoked: Nielsen #3 (user control and freedom) and #5 (error prevention) + Every ASK says USE · NOT-use · reversibility (paul-stated 2026-09-05) + A correct 'no' still owes a next move (cross-project)
findings.recommendation: Ship it at the BOTTOM of account settings, quiet and word-led, in the neutral outlined grammar — never the affirmative fill, which means *recorded*. It must state its consequence before it acts: one line naming that there is no password reset and that getting back in starts with an email to Paul. For the 'please don't contact me' reader that line is not optional — it is her only route and she has no other copy of it. ⛔ If that consequence line cannot be written and reviewed this week, cut sign-out entirely rather than ship the control without it; the shared-device risk is already mitigated by the owner guard, and an unguarded sign-out creates a worse failure than it prevents.

findings.observation: WHAT SHOULD NOT SHIP IN PASS 1. Five acts across four surfaces, for a reader at depth-1, with one real outside user arriving this week. The temptation is to build the graph completely; the graph is worth almost nothing until the two edits people have actually asked for exist.
findings.user_impact: Every surface that ships half-built spends Bob's first impression on a control that does not work. He gets one first week.
findings.principle_invoked: Content and function first; form follows (cross-project) + Build doors on measured demand (memory, paul-approved 2026-08-28) + defer-affordances-pending-signal
findings.recommendation: PASS 1 — ship exactly this: (a) the estate's utility row (`‹ Your homes` / `Settings`) — F5; (b) the list at one home with the coloured row, the `＋ Add a home` row and its honest destination, and `Your account ›` at the bottom — F1/F6; (c) the sign-in branch on `estates.length` — F2; (d) PLACE SETTINGS with NAME + COLOUR + back only — Paul's own stated minimum, and the loop-close in F8 is the whole payoff; (e) ACCOUNT SETTINGS with HOW TO REACH YOU + username-shown + back — F7. ⛔ CUT FROM PASS 1, each with its reason: **address editing** — highest-value edit in the product and the closest call on this list, but it is the s2 field group plus addressParts plus a round trip, and the arrival page's note-box link is honest in the meantime because it says what it is. Pass 2, and soon. **Ranking editing** — 11 tappable items that change nothing visible today; the arrival page already plays the ranking back honestly. **Password change** — there is no reset; half a mechanism is worse than a stated absence. **Sign out** — only with its consequence line (F10). **Any colour picker on account settings** — cut by ruling (F3). **A places-list stop at one home** — cut by ruling (F2). **Any badge, count, status or 'last opened' on a list row.** **Any disclosure on either settings page.** **A second 'delete / share / people / export' section on either page.** **A fifth feedback affordance** (F12).

findings.observation: FOUR NEW SURFACES IS FOUR NEW CHANCES TO MINT A FIFTH FEEDBACK CONTROL. Onboarding carries `.fblink` (quiet underlined line, closed by default, records the screen). estate/index.html carries the same shape. The viewer carries `.feedback-ribbon` — a persistent bookmark tab with a 💬 glyph, always visible. That inconsistency across the handoff was F11 in this morning's review and is still Paul's to rule.
findings.user_impact: Two affordances for one job, one tap apart, is the fastest way to teach a new reader that the app is several apps. Four more surfaces makes it six.
findings.principle_invoked: One shell, one signal each (fernwood candidate) + Nielsen #4
findings.recommendation: Every new surface here either carries the EXISTING `.fblink` shape verbatim, closed by default, or carries nothing. Nothing new is designed. My read stands from this morning: the onboarding/arrival version is the better-designed one on two measurable counts — closed by default, and it records the screen, which is the half that turns 'this is confusing' into a punch-list row. The `+` destination in F1 is a feedback POST wearing a purpose-built label, which is fine and is not a second channel: it uses the same endpoint, the same send component and the same `done(ok)`.

findings.observation: THE EVIDENCE I WAS SENT TO READ IS NOT THERE, AND IT MATTERS FOR WHAT I CAN CLAIM. All four `2026-09-06T13*/REPORT.md` files — mom, owner, strict, wide-eyed — still carry the `WALK-REPORT-UNWRITTEN` marker and contain only the template. `walk-integrity.py` exists precisely to refuse a run in that state, and CLAUDE.md records why: on 2026-09-05 a 287-byte stub was counted as a seat that had reported. The WRITTEN set is `2026-09-06T124x`, and it predates the current arrival page — the strict seat reports that the contact preference 'isn't referenced at all' on the last screen, which is FALSE of the build now on disk, where `How to reach you` is a rendered row.

And does the 'How to reach you' row now change the strict seat's reported unease, which is the only thing in the corpus that tests the highest-stakes field in the product. ⚠️ Also worth noting on its own: three of today's runs are `owner` alone (135556, 135827, 135954, 140321) with no report on any of them — a seat re-run four times and never asked to speak is exactly the shape `walk-integrity` was built to catch.

findings.observation: BUILD THE LIST AGAINST THE PLURAL CONTRACT THAT ALREADY EXISTS. `/api/grant/whoami` returns `estates: [{ estateId, relationship, capability }]` — an array (worker.js:625), and the sign-in response builds the same shape. It will hold exactly one entry until per-request scope lands.
findings.user_impact: None today. The point is that the day scope lands, nothing on the surface should need to change — the list renders what the array holds, and a second entry simply appears.

findings.recommendation: Render the list by iterating `estates`, and derive the sign-in branch from `estates.length` (F2) — never from a hardcoded single-home assumption, never from `estates[0]` with a comment saying 'for now'. This costs nothing today and is the difference between the second home being a surface change and a data change. principles_to_propose.principle: A conditional STOP is not a conditional CONTROL. When a surface is both a chooser and the only door to an action, 'hide it when there is nothing to choose' applies to interposing it in the journey — never to reaching it. The chooser's presence is derived; the door's presence is unconditional.
principles_to_propose.rationale: This is the exact seam on which R1-SA was superseded rather than falsified. Its rule — 'one glyph, absent at one grant' — was correct for a pure switcher and becomes a dead end the moment the same surface also carries founding, because it disappears for precisely the readers who need the thing it holds. The discrimination between the two cases is what neither the original recommendation nor 'build doors on measured demand' can make. 1 occurrence (2026-09-06, the places list). Watch for a second on any Fernwood surface that is a chooser and a creator at once.

principles_to_propose.principle: Two parents means two surfaces, not one surface with a memory. When one screen would be reachable from two places and must return to whichever it came from, prefer splitting it by the OBJECT it edits — because a back control that names its destination in words needs no stored origin, and an origin that is stored can be wrong.
principles_to_propose.rationale: Proposed as a cross-project candidate because it is a pure IA move with no Fernwood content in it. Paul named the requirement himself in 19c ('go back cannot be a hardcoded destination') and treated it as a state problem; the cheaper answer is that the requirement is usually a symptom of a wrongly-merged surface. The tell: the two entry points edit different OBJECTS (a person vs a place). Where they genuinely edit the same object, the origin is real and must be stored. 1 occurrence — 2026-09-06, account settings vs place settings.

principles_to_propose.principle: An identity token belongs to the thing it distinguishes. A colour, glyph or name that exists so a reader can tell N instances apart must be a property of the INSTANCE, never of the person viewing them — a per-person token makes every instance look the same at exactly the moment there is more than one.
principles_to_propose.rationale: Sharpens 'Ornament earns its place' with a test that has a right answer rather than a judgement: ask what the element DISTINGUISHES, and put it there. It also caught something a precedence rule would have missed — the account-level accent is not merely redundant at two homes, it is a net loss, because it destroys the only pre-literate wayfinding signal available at half-engagement. 1 occurrence — 2026-09-06, the `accent` / `identity.theme.main` collision (BACKLOG 19c). Likely second occurrence: any Bolo Boys surface where a per-show identity competes with a site-wide one.

principles_to_propose.principle: CONFIRMING OCCURRENCE with a sharpening — 'Save-success at the surface, not at the destination' (cross-project, canon since 2026-07-07). The sharpening: the strongest save-success is a DESTINATION THAT HAS ALREADY CHANGED. Where an edit surface returns to a parent that renders the edited value, the confirmation at the control exists only to cover the moment before the return; the return trip itself is the receipt.
principles_to_propose.rationale: Second occurrence outside the original Garden Guru case, and the first where the destination is a surface the value actually PAINTS — change the place's name or colour, tap back, and the masthead you return to is already different. Worth adding to the existing principle's Why rather than filing anything new: it names the case where the rule is nearly free, and it is the argument for putting the name and colour first in place settings rather than last.
